result.topic_en: The page finishes an optical (lens) calculation with a condition linking the data a, b, c, c', n, n', f, then begins a derivation of Lagrange's series-inversion theorem for the special case x = t + u x^λ.
result.transcription:
273
$p-q' = a+b-c'$
$p'-q = a+b-c$
Also
$a+b-c' = (n-\frac{1}{n'})f = \frac{nn'-1}{n'}f$
$a+b-c = (n'-\frac{1}{n})f = \frac{nn'-1}{n}f$
Zwischen den Daten muss also die Gleichung
Statt finden
$(a+b-c')n' = (a+b-c)n$
Im Fall $c=c'$ muss auch $n=n'$ sein
und man hat dann
$a+b-c = (n-\frac{1}{n})f$

Fr
Lagrange's Lehrsatz
auf möglich lichtvollste Art abgeleitet.
(Verglichen S. 94.
I. Specieller Fall.
Grundgleichung $x = t + ux^{\lambda}$
Gesucht
$x^n = t^n + T_1 u + T_2 uu + T_3 u^3 + \text{u.s.w.}$
Hier sind $T_1$, $T_2$, $T_3$ u.s.w. Functionen von $t$, die in
$\Theta_1$, $\Theta_2$, $\Theta_3$ u.s.w. übergehen mögen, wenn man
anstatt $n$, so weit es in ihnen vorkommt, $n+\lambda$ schreibt.
Man hat also offenbar
$x^{n+\lambda} = t^{n+\lambda} + \Theta_1 u + \Theta_2 uu + \Theta_3 u^3 + \text{u.s.w.}$
Allgemein ist, für irgend eine Function [-von x,-] $Fx$ von $x$
$\frac{dFx}{du} = x^{\lambda}\cdot\frac{dFx}{dt}$

methods.what: Expressions for a+b-c and a+b-c' in terms of the refractive quantities n, n' and the focal length f (optics)
Consistency condition that the data must satisfy
Special case c = c', which forces n = n'
Lagrange inversion theorem: power-series expansion of x^n in u, where x = t + u x^λ
methods.quote: $x^n = t^n + T_1 u + T_2 uu + T_3 u^3 + \text{u.s.w.}$

methods.what: Expansion of x^{n+λ} obtained by replacing n with n+λ in the coefficients
Partial-derivative relation for any function of the implicitly defined x
